title: CLO 2024 Academic Month: Exploration of CLO in Structural and Structural Creativity Teaching
description: Review of CLO Academic Month 2024! A conversation with Professor Gao Yiwen from Henan University of Engineering, sharing teaching experiences of directly instructing students in pattern making within the CLO 2D window: combining 2D pattern pieces with corresponding 3D effects to assist students in understanding, learning, practicing, and designing. Skillfully using a one-student-one-design practice strategy to encourage students to learn independently, learn from each other, and expand into different styles.
transcript:
Thank you, Colo, for giving me the opportunity to share some of my teaching work here.  
The theme of my sharing is the exploration of Clo in structural and structural innovation teaching.  
It is mainly divided into four aspects.  
The first is to introduce the global sustainability wave and the problems of existing structures and structural teaching.  
The second is the auxiliary function and practice of modeling software in structural teaching.  
The third is the practical thinking behind gradually introducing modeling software in early-stage structural classes.  
The fourth is the interest it brings to other courses.  

First, regarding the global sustainability wave and the problems of existing structures and structural teaching, we divide it into three parts.  
The first is the global sustainability wave and the problems of existing structures and structural teaching, as well as issues with teaching practical capabilities.  
The second is the global sustainability wave and the problems of existing structures and structural teaching.  
I believe everyone has reached a consensus on this.  
For example, the overproduction of clothing in the fashion industry certainly causes issues regarding waste conversion.  
The industry must shift from the traditional high-performance and high-discharge mode to a more environmentally friendly and sustainable development model.  
In the future, as the population grows,  
it is possible that the clothing industry will become the top contributor to pollution.  
Currently, the fashion industry is already the second largest polluter globally.  
With population growth, for example, by 2030,  
the United Nations predicts the global population will reach 8.5 billion.  
This population increase will also increase clothing consumption.  
Under these circumstances, it is possible that clothing will surpass the food industry, currently the largest polluter worldwide.  

Also, in the process of designing and modifying clothing,  
we must first design the fabric.  
Only through fabric design can we improve clothing and product details.  
However, design itself is a form of consumption.  
AI also impacts this process.  
We all know that AI has been very popular since last year.  
It has a significant impact on the clothing industry.  
AI can quickly generate clothing effects,  
but it cannot solve very specific parameter details.  
3D can achieve a closer-to-reality effect.  
AI can generate the clothing effect,  
but it cannot produce a physical sample.  
Therefore, samples are needed to address this.  
With clothing modeling software,  
we can make specific and detailed adjustments to this reality.  
Hence, we use AI to create an ideal image,  
and 3D to make specific and detailed adjustments.  
This is one of the most environmentally friendly approaches.  
I believe we all agree on these points.  

Now, I would like to discuss the problems existing in our design and design teaching.  
For example, our design courses are compressed with other overall teaching classes.  
For example, at our school,  
there are probably about 170 design classes.  
I guess other primary schools are also within this range,  
because there are other courses as well.  
In these 170 classes, students must master very complex and varied styles,  
and practice many styles and detailed craftsmanship.  
That means the time is very limited,  
but industry demands require students to master  
and have sufficient structural knowledge.  
Then, in design, painting, craftsmanship, or other fields,  
they can have a solid professional foundation.  

So, after the class compression,  
how can we enable students to master more solid structural knowledge  
within a short class duration?  
This is very important.  

Also, there is a lack of practical ability.  
Because there are fewer classes, students practice less,  
and for clothing,  
we must convert some sample data into real garments.  
This connection requires hands-on experience  
to foster better understanding.  
Without practice, this understanding is insufficient.  

Also, different fabrics need to be produced  
so students can understand their effects.  
The same style  
with different fabrics  
may produce different results.  
This also requires practice and production to achieve proficiency.  

Additionally, our comprehensive course load is relatively dense.  
If the course load is heavy,  
there is less time for practice at school.  
The overall practice time is relatively short.  
With limited practice time,  
the final professional ability might lag behind.  

In design classes,  
students also have many design projects to complete and practice.  
However, the finished products often lack thoughtful consideration.  
There is always a significant gap  
between the effect images and the final product imagination.  
The application of patterns, colors, and designs  
may not be particularly suitable,  
resulting in a finished product that is not ideal.  

We all judge based on effect images or sketches  
to decide whether a garment needs adjustment,  
or which parts need modification.  
But the sketches, effect images, and real clothing  
are often understood differently by different people.  
There is this gap.  

Therefore, repeated experimentation and reflection are necessary.  
Only then can decisions be made  
on how to adjust details.  
Due to a lack of structural practice,  
there is no confidence in pattern making.  
This leads to external issues.  

I think this problem exists in many schools nationwide.  
Many students can do the work independently,  
but many students, especially after graduating from design programs,  
experience external problems.  
Even in early courses, external issues can arise.  
This phenomenon is very detrimental.  

Additionally, there is a problem with teachers' practical abilities.  
Many of our teachers enter schools right after graduating from college.  
In society,  
they rarely engage in practical design or pattern-making experience.  
Thus, the knowledge they bring back to school is mostly theoretical.  
This lack of practical experience is a problem.  

Family responsibilities also affect teachers.  
Many teachers in the clothing profession are female.  
They have to care for children and the elderly.  
All of this takes up a lot of their time,  
limiting their personal space.  
Our college teachers generally do not teach many classes.  
If they want to practice at home,  
there may be many inconveniences.  
Sufficient space and time are required to practice.  
Balancing family and work is a challenge.  
We need to improve our professionalism rapidly.  

We also need to consider new ways of dissemination.  
For example, we now have many social media platforms such as Xiaohongshu and Bilibili.  
In this era of self-media,  
students have increasing expectations of teachers.  
Many online bloggers in specific fields  
demonstrate excellent professional characteristics.  
Students have access to more and better professional experts online,  
which raises their expectations for offline teachers.  

For college teachers,  
how can we establish ourselves as professionals with strong capabilities in certain fields?  
In all aspects,  
the professional depth and practical ability of teachers  
are significantly different from before.  

Now, modeling software can help us solve many of the previous problems.  
Modeling software mainly supports structural teaching and practice.  
First, it supports structural teaching and some practical aspects of structural instruction.  
Because from the very first semester,  
we have introduced modeling software when students start structural classes.  
We use Clo 3D.  
I will also discuss practices and uses in this regard.  

Modeling software helps students explore structure after class.  
It can also improve teachers' structural and creative practices.  
Let's divide these into two parts.  
First, modeling software assists structural teaching.  
It allows visualization, is intuitive, and can operate in real time.  
I think all teachers who have used 3D modeling software have a deep understanding of this.  

For example, the visualization of shapes and human body forms in virtual mannequins,  
adjusting model sizes,  
we can get models of different shapes.  

Visualizing the relationship between structure and materials is also very important.  
And attempting diversification.  
If we want to try very creative, complex, or simple models,  
we can present them in real time through this software.  

Students can learn structure during the learning process.  
They need such a tool to help achieve this.  
There is also increased efficiency in reducing costs and enhancing learning.  
If we use physical fabric,  
early investments are very high.  

For example, if you go to a structural class and make a sample,  
if you make all models physically,  
students might have to make them for you.  

Next, starting from first grade,  
we introduce modeling software presentations from prototypes.  
Now, every school has its own digital teaching platform,  
such as learning communication, smart classrooms, language classes, etc.  

Our school uses a digital learning platform.  
This platform is not only for teaching but also for administration.  
When we use this digital platform,  
we also introduce new technologies such as modeling software.  

If you want to teach digitally,  
you can use the digital platform.  
At the same time, we use the 2D window in the 3D software for the drawing process.  

In this way, students and their partners will not only complete their structural drawings by hand but also use the 3D 2D board tool to create corresponding structural drawings or meet work requirements.  

You can see this is the basic prototype and the A-type group.  
At the same time, there is also a rotating 3D effect of the basic model.  

As the structural class progresses, we move from the prototype, parts, contact groups, structure, to jackets and more complex structures.  
For example, the contact group is more complicated.  
We can show the effect of release and the effect after hitting the butterfly knot.  
This kind of display is more intuitive.  
You don’t have to make a finished product and carry it back and forth.  

Previously, I used to make finished products before and after class.  
Now, students can study the structural relationships during class.  

Okay, that was a simple introduction.  
Next, I will discuss some exercises introduced using 3D software in structural teaching.  

First, from the prototype, we generally ask students to build three sets of virtual models and prototypes.  
Anyone who has used 3D software knows that virtual model sizes can be adjusted.  

So, first, each student builds their own virtual model,  
virtual measurements, and virtual prototype.  
They design and prepare clothing for themselves.  
Then, they build for family members.  

Because in structural classes,  
for example, I first went to the Nanxi library.  
Following the Nanxi library process,  
most students are willing to do it for their family or themselves.  

Previously, when the teacher finished a sample of the Nanxi library in class,  
different students inserted family or their own sizes into it.  
If it’s your own size, it’s easy;  
if it’s a family member’s size, problems arise.  
For example, family members might live far away,  
and measurements may be inaccurate, especially in specific cases.  

The teacher might suggest students have their family members measured carefully before starting,  
for better fitting clothes such as pants or shirts.  

However, family measurements may still be inaccurate,  
leading to final garments that don’t fit well.  

If the teacher cannot check carefully,  
some sizes might be missed,  
causing the finished sample to be unsuitable for the family member.  

Therefore, we build virtual sizes and virtual prototypes for family members.  
Once these sizes are accurately established,  
students can produce more accurate garments for themselves or their families.  

Then, there is the virtual size and prototype for models.  
When graduating from design,  
we usually invite models for performances,  
and the model’s size must match the garment size.  

Sometimes, mid-level design classes also hold performances with invited models.  
Although sizes vary, models are usually about 175 cm tall, for example.  

After establishing these three sizes — personal, family, and model —  
we can use the model’s size in design processes or social practices.  
We can directly use the model’s size in the 2D window of Clo 3D for pattern making.  

Some friends may ask, after pattern making, how to print the paper patterns?  
Our software and many 3D programs support DXF or PLT formats.  
If you export in these formats,  
you can print the paper patterns and cut fabric directly.  

Now, what we show next:  
At our school, the first class covers roundness and rotation;  
the second class covers pants.  

For pants,  
the first class talks about pants structure,  
and the next covers the pants manufacturing process.  

Typically, many students make pants for their fathers.  
We show two examples here: one for a fat father, the other for a lean father.  

Before pattern making,  
we first build a virtual body for the father,  
a virtual human body with adjusted size,  
a virtual prototype.  

After building the virtual prototype,  
we start pattern making.  
After making the pattern,  
we try it on.  

If the father is not satisfied — pants too short, leg size, waist size —  
questions arise: Is the leg fat or thin? Is the waist fat?  
Do clothes need to be for winter? Wool pants?  

After considering all factors,  
we adjust again using 3D software  
until the father is satisfied with the fit.  

These practices are done by second-year students.  
After adjustments,  
we use cutting machines to make samples, cut fabric,  
and proceed to craft classes.  

After craft classes,  
the pants adapt well to the father’s size.  
Compared to before, the process is more intuitive  
and communication with family members is easier.  

We can also note that Clo 3D and other modeling software will impact the customization industry.  

For example, with the fat father’s model,  
we can rotate to see the back or other views.  
The father can see and say what fits or not —  
pants too short, long, or loose — and communicate adjustments.  

My approach is to make it more comfortable for the student.  
Before making the pattern,  
I let students make a sample in the 2D window,  
then show it in the 3D window.  

When teachers check the work,  
they must carefully review the 2D basic pattern,  
because in traditional methods, you might have to measure bit by bit manually.  
In the software, you can directly measure and check if the pattern has issues —  
circumference, leg opening size, dart size, single curve size, etc.  

The software also allows self-checking through 3D fitting simulations.  
However, teachers still need to carefully inspect,  
because inexperienced users might miss issues.  

You can see the thin model here;  
besides family measurements, students also create accurate personal virtual sizes and prototypes.  
This allows accurate personal garment creation.  

Before making a physical garment,  
you can view the virtual effect in the 3D window.  
You can see which areas satisfy or dissatisfy you and adjust accordingly.  
This adjustment is quite accurate.  

Some friends mentioned learning CAD, but we rarely use CAD now,  
because if students have to learn CAD, Clo, and structure simultaneously,  
the workload is too much.  
So now, we mainly make patterns in the 2D window,  
not in CAD.  
After making patterns in the 2D window,  
we directly fit and simulate.  

The size and shape of virtual mannequins differ from the default.  
Why? Because students adjust the virtual mannequins according to their own measurements.  
They are more passionate about making clothes for themselves.  

Overall, we introduce Clo or other 3D software into structural courses using 3D mannequins.  

Now, let’s take a look at the gradual, progressive, and sustainable introduction of modeling software in structural teaching.  
We know structural courses begin in the first and second years,  
continuing through the third year,  
usually spanning three to four semesters,  
with each semester having about 30 to 60 class hours.  

The process starts with building personal prototypes,  
practice in rotation,  
then pants for men and women.  
Structural courses progress gradually and deeply,  
covering continuous groups, collars,  
shirt structures, coats, and creative structural changes.  

At the same time, software use deepens progressively.  

Students restore pants structures to fit their own sizes.  
This size is not the default model size.  

When teaching pants, teachers discuss typical cases, usually two or three styles.  
But to have students master more styles, what to do?  
Previously, students practiced more independently.  
Now, each student is assigned a style, selected by the teacher.  

Teachers select styles for students to restore.  
Students find styles online,  
then restore them, adjusting for fit and authenticity.  

Students have made adjustments; some use their sizes, some use model sizes.  

What are the benefits of one student per style?  
It avoids uniformity;  
if we gave electronic assignments,  
there is a risk of copying.  
With one style per student,  
and requiring original files and renderings,  
each student focuses on their own work.  

Most students live in dorms, with 4 to 6 people per room.  
Discussions naturally happen when someone struggles or has questions.  
This peer discussion helps deepen understanding of different styles.  
This saves teachers from having to teach every style in class, which is impossible due to time constraints.  

Such discussions promote learning among students.  

Here are some continuous group structural exercises done by second-year students.  
These are structural exercises on continuous groups.  
It’s impossible to teach all styles during class, so only classic cases are introduced.  
Students encounter many questions with variant styles.  

Here is practice on collar parts.  
Each student has a different collar style — lapel collar, flat collar, etc.  
Students practice independently.  

For example, a second-year student working on a lapel collar started with one version, felt something was off,  
made another version, compared them,  
and decided which was more accurate, discarding the original.  

This process is not teacher-directed corrections, but self-driven exploration and modification.  

This happens in real-time with pattern display effects, which is much stronger than hand-drawing.  
It saves time compared to making physical garments.  

Once students master basic tools,  
their after-class structural exploration improves significantly.  

Second-year students also did small holiday exercises.  
These are simple styles, but students experiment with patterns and fabrics.  

One student made a horse-face skirt with background settings during the winter break.  
These are self-designed styles and self-made patterns.  
Some have flaws and issues, but the general direction is correct.  
Detailed issues still require making physical samples to experience.  

3D cannot replace the fundamentals of structural principles, which students must still master.  
Mastering structure is very important.  
Once structure is mastered, changing colors or fabrics can be quickly displayed in 3D.  

Especially now, with AI, structure and craftsmanship become even more important.  
After mastering modeling software,  
teachers also greatly improve their practical ability in structure and structural creativity.  

Here is some work I did during the holiday.  
This is a 2024 Autumn/Winter piece by Issey Miyake.  
I explored and recreated it.  
You can’t really understand the design without making it.  
After making it, you realize how clever the designer is.  

For example, why one pocket is present but another is not —  
because two pockets waste fabric, whereas one pocket fits perfectly in the fabric layout, saving material.  
After making it, you truly understand the design.  

This is an asymmetric pleated skirt structure reproduction of Issey Miyake.  
At first, the style seems interesting but hard to make.  
Can it be realized?  
It’s basically made from rectangular pieces of fabric.  
After practicing, you really grasp the design’s essence.  

Here are two reproductions from the ethnic costume museum’s collection.  
One is inspired by Julian Roberts’ subtraction techniques,  
another is a practice in ready-to-wear dress structure.  
There is also a practice inspired by traditional lace patterns.  

Traditional lace strips are rectangular fabric strips sewn together.  
Ethnic costumes have embroidery.  
The museum’s electronic collection displays are excellent,  
and these can be handled and recreated in Clo.  

Here is a series of structural experiments inspired by the “Seven-Bridge” pattern.  
We now advocate for sustainability and environmental protection.  
The Seven-Bridge pattern is a zero-waste rectangular fabric segmentation.  
Can we turn it into clothing?  
This is my personal experiment.  

We all know “Bai Ku Yao” pants,  
which consist of a rectangular piece of fabric folded three times.  
I learned about this structure from teacher Liu Ruipu’s book on ethnic costumes.  
Based on this structure, I made pants,  
longer than the Bai Ku Yao pants,  
and inspired a top.  

This is also a zero-waste structural experiment.  

Here is an attempt at offset stitching.  
In design, besides patterns and colors, there are many structural design possibilities.  
For example, offset stitching.  
The skirt’s sequin pieces are normally sewn aligned,  
but I sewed them offset,  
creating a different effect.  

Design inspired by structure is a very important design method.  

Saving material, minimizing space and time,  
while balancing housework,  
I think this is the biggest advantage of modeling software.  
Since learning modeling software, I really love it.  

Now, let me share some early-stage practices and thoughts on gradually introducing modeling software in structural classes.  

First, I will introduce some modeling software functions used in early structural classes,  
and then discuss electronic assignment plagiarism prevention methods.  

In early structural classes, we mainly introduce 2D pattern making,  
how to make patterns in the 2D window,  
as well as cutting functions and others.  

These functions perfectly match structural needs.  

Mainly used 2D functions include:  
- Point selection and division  
- Rotation of points and lines  
- Length adjustment of line segments  
- Angles  
- Basic seam lines  

In 3D, the most basic tools include adjusting virtual mannequin size.  
After adjustment, you must save the size to use next time.  

Other basic features in the 3D toolbar include simulation and rendering functions.  

In the first structural class, due to limited hours, we do not change the original schedule.  
In the second structural class, we introduce more functions,  
including rendering, screen recording simulation, colors, patterns, etc.  

This is a gradual introduction.  
At first, it may not be perfect, but interest grows as students see results.  

Now, about electronic assignment plagiarism prevention.  
Because assignments are electronic,  
we teach students to submit original files and renderings.  
As mentioned, each student has one style.  

Here are two images given to students, along with a link to detailed style information, including material descriptions.  
Students can simulate original materials.  

For complex pants styles, teachers cannot cover all in class.  
So students explore and investigate independently.  
If they don’t understand, they ask.  

This is a student relay in a WeChat group, where students choose their styles honestly.  
If students choose themselves, they may pick very simple ones.  
If assigned, they can be given medium-difficulty styles, which challenge them appropriately.  

Each student’s style is different.  
This increases teachers’ workload, because each student encounters unique problems, mostly structural, but also software-related.  

During style selection, some software functions may not be covered by teachers initially.  
As students encounter issues, teachers explain them later.  
Students gradually master software and become more proficient.  

In dorms, as styles differ, students discuss and help each other in groups.  
This deepens understanding of structure and software use.  

Although teachers work harder initially,  
students benefit greatly.  
Once students master tools, their autonomy increases.  

Here is a skirt exercise done by second-year students during vacation.  
The skirt style was AI-generated, then modeled in 3D.  
I helped adjust minor parts and rendered it because many students’ computers have limited capacity.  
I provided a large render image.  

Once students master structure and software,  
other courses also benefit.  
For example, design courses gain strong support,  
and material courses also improve.  

Many students, especially design majors, find materials difficult by senior year.  
They dislike memorizing.  
Actually, repeated use leads to natural familiarity.  

Also, building a 3D database for the class helps later design work.  
We will discuss this later.  

Here is a design course auxiliary example.  
A design student made some sketches, then simulated one style.  
After simulation, the student immediately sees if the chest area is suitable or not.  
Even without teacher review, the student understands this.  

Here are design course sketches.  
If a teacher were to select, some sketches would be rejected due to poor feasibility or appearance.  
However, once students master the software, they can try independently.  

This student used arcs and circles to try designs.  
The process yields great learning outcomes.  

Also, it encourages exploration and trying different structures, which is very beneficial.  

This is a sketch exercise by a second-year design student.  
They selected a style and simulated the effect.  

This process, especially in the first design class,  
helps students virtually realize their ideas,  
reducing waste of physical samples.  

It also facilitates adjustments to details,  
since sketches and finished products differ in detail.  

This is particularly good for custom clothing.  
With 3D software,  
after graduation or in enterprises,  
students or individuals can try this approach.  

For material courses, taught in the first semester of the second year,  
if students do not use the software regularly, they will forget.  

However, 3D software has a materials library.  
By clicking and selecting,  
material names and properties are displayed.  

This process strengthens memory through repeated use,  
enhancing knowledge of fabrics and patterns.  

After a few years, students will find materials less daunting.  
They can try different fabric patterns, colors, and textures.  

In design courses, after the first or second class,  
pattern design and application in clothing are taught.  
Previously, pattern and effect images were created separately.  
Matching them perfectly was difficult.  

Now, using 3D software,  
materials and patterns can be intuitively displayed.  
You can adjust pattern size, color, and position,  
tweaking until satisfied.  

Our material printing function allows exporting patterned files suitable for digital printing.  

Another point:  
from the beginning of using Clo 3D,  
we build a class 3D database,  
since each student makes one style.  

This database contains pants, dresses, coats, etc.  
Later, for integrated design, it becomes very convenient.  
You can just modify an existing pattern.  

For example, if your design focus is a top,  
and your pants are bell-bottoms or paper-bag style,  
you can find a suitable style in the class database, adjust it, and the pattern is ready.  

This greatly improves design efficiency.  

Besides the class database,  
the software’s marketplace also has rich 3D style resources.  
We can take these and make appropriate adjustments,  
further accelerating design conversion.  

This will definitely make design faster and richer.  

Some may worry about job loss,  
but faster design means a richer market with more styles.  

As mentioned, customization becomes possible.  
Previously, large-batch customization was common for suits or shirts.  
Now, software may enable custom women’s wear as well.  

Finally, I want to discuss an unavoidable topic: the impact of AI on design.  

During the industrial era, mechanical manufacturing accelerated ready-to-wear production.  
Combined with human desire for novelty and differentiation,  
large batch orders have shrunk and continue to shrink.  

Entering the AI era, with increasingly broad AI applications,  
we must think about the direction of design development.  

For example, this is an AI-generated image,  
and this is a 3D-rendered version.  

AI is a tool,  
but hand drawing and other methods remain necessary.  
If there is no specific design goal, AI is very powerful.  
But with specific requirements, AI has limitations.  

AI’s spatial understanding is also weak.  
For example, if I ask AI to generate a circular cutting continuous pattern,  
it cannot produce it.  
Anything related to cutting and structure,  
except for regular styles or minor creative variations,  
AI currently struggles.  

This concludes my recent work sharing.

chunks.title: CLO 2024 Academic Month: Exploration of CLO in Structural and Structural Creativity Teaching
chunks.content: ## Exploration of CLO in Structural and Structural Creativity Teaching This document covers the integration of CLO 3D modeling software in structural and creative fashion design education. It addresses global sustainability challenges, problems in traditional structural teaching, practical applications of modeling software, progressive teaching strategies, and the impact of AI on design workflows. --- ## Global Sustainability Challenges and Issues in Structural Teaching This section discusses the environmental impact of the fashion industry, the limitations of traditional design teaching, and the need for improved practical skills and sustainable development in clothing production. The fashion industry is currently the second largest global polluter and is projected to worsen with population growth, potentially surpassing the food industry by 2030 when the global population is expected to reach 8.5 billion. Overproduction in fashion leads to significant waste, necessitating a shift from high-performance, high-discharge manufacturing modes to more sustainable practices. Clothing design starts with fabric design, which directly influences garment quality and detail. However, design itself consumes resources. The rise of AI has accelerated clothing effect generation but lacks precision in parameter specifics and cannot produce physical samples. In contrast, 3D modeling software like CLO 3D enables realistic fabric and garment simulations, allowing detailed adjustments that are crucial for sustainable prototyping. Combining AI-generated conceptual images with 3D adjustments represents an environmentally friendly approach to design. Traditional design education faces challenges including compressed course hours, dense curricula, and insufficient time for hands-on practice. Students often lack practical experience necessary for converting samples into real garments, understanding fabric effects, and mastering detailed craftsmanship. This gap affects student confidence and leads to discrepancies between design sketches and final products. Additionally, many teachers lack practical industry experience, and personal constraints such as family responsibilities limit their capacity to practice and improve professionally. The rise of social media platforms has raised students' expectations for teachers, who must now demonstrate strong professional and practical capabilities to remain credible in the digital age. --- ## Auxiliary Functions and Practices of Modeling Software in Structural Teaching This section explores how CLO 3D modeling software enhances structural teaching by improving visualization, practice efficiency, and creative exploration in fashion education. Modeling software supports structural teaching by enabling intuitive, real-time visualization of garment shapes and virtual mannequins. It allows adjustments of model sizes and fabric-material relationships, facilitating experimentation with complex or simple designs without the need for physical samples. This reduces costs and increases efficiency. From the first semester, students use CLO 3D to complement traditional pattern drafting, combining 2D drawing tools with 3D simulation. This dual approach enables students to produce virtual prototypes for themselves, family members, and models, addressing challenges such as inaccurate measurements and fitting issues. Virtual prototypes ensure more precise garment creation and facilitate communication in custom garment making. The software supports exporting patterns in DXF or PLT formats for printing and fabric cutting, bridging the gap between digital design and physical sample production.

chunks.content: From the first semester, students use CLO 3D to complement traditional pattern drafting, combining 2D drawing tools with 3D simulation. This dual approach enables students to produce virtual prototypes for themselves, family members, and models, addressing challenges such as inaccurate measurements and fitting issues. Virtual prototypes ensure more precise garment creation and facilitate communication in custom garment making. The software supports exporting patterns in DXF or PLT formats for printing and fabric cutting, bridging the gap between digital design and physical sample production. Example applications include pants design classes where students create virtual bodies for clients (e.g., family members), adjust patterns in 3D, and refine garments based on virtual fittings. This iterative process enhances fitting accuracy and student understanding while streamlining sample production. Teachers emphasize careful review of 2D patterns within the software to identify issues such as circumference, leg opening size, and darts, supplemented by 3D fitting simulations. Structural design courses typically span three to four semesters with 30-60 class hours each. The curriculum begins with personal virtual prototype construction and progresses to more complex garments such as pants, continuous groups, collars, shirts, coats, and creative structural modifications. Each student is assigned a unique style to restore and modify using CLO 3D, preventing plagiarism and fostering individual exploration. This approach also promotes peer discussion in dormitory settings, enhancing collaborative problem-solving and deepening structural understanding. Exercises include continuous group structures and collar variations where students independently iterate on designs, self-assessing and refining their patterns without direct teacher corrections. This real-time, software-assisted approach is more efficient and effective than traditional hand-drawing or physical prototyping. Holiday and out-of-class exercises encourage students to experiment with new styles and fabrics, reinforcing learning. While 3D software enhances visualization and prototyping, fundamental mastery of structural principles remains essential. --- ## Structural Creativity and Advanced Applications Using CLO 3D This section highlights examples of creative structural experiments and reproductions using CLO 3D, demonstrating the software’s role in advancing design understanding and sustainability. Recreations include a 2024 Autumn/Winter asymmetric pleated skirt by Issey Miyake, showcasing how practical garment construction reveals design ingenuity such as fabric-saving pocket placement. Other projects reproduce traditional ethnic costumes using subtraction techniques, ready-to-wear structures, and lace patterns sourced from museum collections. Sustainability-driven experiments focus on zero-waste designs like the "Seven-Bridge" rectangular fabric segmentation and adaptations inspired by Bai Ku Yao pants, which use folded rectangular fabric pieces to minimize waste. Offset stitching techniques are explored to create novel visual effects in sequin skirts, illustrating structural design’s creative potential. These projects underline the advantages of modeling software in saving material, time, and effort, while balancing academic responsibilities.
